passage: Ankita, you froze when the director praised your report, so let me tell you about mine. I'm Francis. At twenty-five I finished a bridge inspection ahead of schedule, and the chief engineer thanked me in front of everyone. My face went hot and I wanted the attention gone, so I said, "Oh, it was nothing, anyone could do it." The chief looked disappointed, and a colleague told me later it felt like I had thrown his thanks back. Years on, when praise came again, I said, "Thank you, sir. It helped that Sajan covered the night readings." Just that. The chief nodded, Sajan grinned, and nobody had to pretend anything. Thank first, then hand out whatever credit is due.

qa.q: What did Francis say when the chief engineer thanked Francis at twenty-five?
qa.a: Francis said, "Oh, it was nothing, anyone could do it."

qa.q: What was Francis feeling when brushing off the thanks?
qa.a: Francis's face went hot and Francis wanted the attention gone, so Francis was probably embarrassed. Modesty is another possible reading.

qa.q: What did Francis change the second time praise came?
qa.a: Francis said thank you first and then gave credit to Sajan for covering the night readings.

qa.q: How did the chief engineer seem to take the first reply?
qa.a: The chief looked disappointed, and Francis was told later that it felt as if the chief's thanks had been thrown back.

grounding: A young adult who once deflected thanks learns to accept recognition with a simple thank-you and credit to others.

passage: The canteen was so loud that Mahima had to lean in to be heard. The maintenance team's shift change was five minutes away, and Deepak was still holding his tray. "The generator fix on Saturday saved our whole batch," Mahima said. "Thank you. Truly." Deepak's first instinct was to laugh it off. Instead he put the tray down and said, "Thank you, that means a lot. Naveen did the wiring, and I handled the testing." Mahima smiled, noted both names for the weekly update, and hurried off. Deepak stood there a second with warm ears, then went to find Naveen to tell him.

qa.q: How soon was the maintenance team's shift change?
qa.a: It was five minutes away.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling as he stood there with warm ears?
qa.a: He felt pleased 😊 and a little shy at being thanked, and he wanted Naveen to hear it too. Warm ears could also just be the heat of the canteen.

qa.q: What made Deepak's reply a good way to accept thanks?
qa.a: He said thank you plainly and named Naveen's wiring, so he neither waved it off nor kept all the credit.

qa.q: How might Mahima have felt if Deepak had laughed it off?
qa.a: Mahima might have felt unheard, as if Mahima's thanks did not count, and been less likely to speak up next time.

grounding: A young adult accepts thanks with a warm acknowledgement and credits another person instead of deflecting or boasting, under time pressure in a noisy place.

passage: Bhupen from accounts. In Thursday's review the regional head asked who had found the mismatch in the vendor payments. Alka could have said "we" and let it blur. Instead she said, "Sameer found it. On Tuesday he noticed the same invoice number in two months, and he traced it back through the ledger before I had even looked. I only wrote the summary." Sameer, two chairs down, straightened up and went pink. The head nodded and noted his name. I wondered whether Alka was being generous or wanted to look fair in front of the head, and I couldn't tell. Later Sameer sent her a thank-you with a 🙂, and Alka forwarded her email to the whole team with his name in the subject.

qa.q: What did Sameer notice on Tuesday?
qa.a: He noticed the same invoice number in two months.

qa.q: How did Bhupen feel about why Alka named Sameer?
qa.a: Bhupen felt unsure, wondering whether Alka was being generous or wanted to look fair in front of the head, and could not tell.

qa.q: What made Alka's credit work better than saying "good team effort"?
qa.a: It was specific, given in the meeting, and said who did what, so the head and the team both knew Sameer's part.

qa.q: How might Sameer have felt when Alka spoke?
qa.a: He straightened up and went pink, so he was probably surprised and pleased, though shy at being named in front of the head.

grounding: A young professional publicly and specifically credits a teammate's contribution in a meeting, seen by a colleague.

passage:
Monday. Jasleen presented the delivery dashboard to the clients and said, "We built this over the last month." Rajni, who had built nearly all of it, kept smiling and looked at the table.
Wednesday. Rajni's replies to Jasleen's messages got short. "All fine," she wrote. Jasleen thought back to the meeting and asked, "Was it the way I described the dashboard?" Rajni said, "A bit. The filter was mine."
Following Tuesday. In the next meeting Jasleen said, "Rajni built the regional filter that shows late deliveries. It cut our weekly report time. Rajni, thank you." Rajni's shoulders dropped, she nodded, and after the meeting she stayed to help with the next slide.

qa.q: Which part of the dashboard did Rajni say was hers?
qa.a: The filter.

qa.q: What was Rajni feeling on Wednesday, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She felt overlooked and a bit hurt, since her replies got short and she wrote "All fine" after looking at the table on Monday. It might also have been workload.

qa.q: What made Jasleen's second mention of the dashboard repair the trust?
qa.a: Jasleen named Rajni, the specific filter and what it achieved, in front of the same kind of group.

qa.q: What would the clients likely have understood on Monday?
qa.a: They would likely have thought both people built it equally, since Jasleen said "We built this."

grounding: A young professional moves from vague shared credit to specific, public credit for a teammate, which repairs trust.

passage: The hospital corridor smelled of disinfectant. Avni sat with her father's file on her knees while her phone buzzed on the bench: a row of heart emojis from the office group, and "thinking of you" from three people. She read them and felt something like gratitude, then a hollow tiredness, because nobody could sit in the corridor for her. Around nine, Jomon from her team walked in with two cups of tea and a phone charger. "I didn't know what to type," he said. "So I came. I can go if you want quiet." Avni hesitated, then moved her bag so he could sit. They didn't talk much. She did not tell him the messages had helped too.

qa.q: What did Jomon bring with him to the hospital?
qa.a: He brought two cups of tea and a phone charger.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling as she read the messages on the bench?
qa.a: Some gratitude mixed with a hollow tiredness, since nobody could sit in the corridor for her. Her hesitation when Jomon arrived may show she was unsure she wanted company.

qa.q: What could Jomon do while sitting with Avni?
qa.a: He can stay quiet unless she wants to talk, and keep checking that she wants him there, as he already offered to leave.

qa.q: How might the colleagues who sent the messages see them?
qa.a: They probably meant them sincerely as quick support from a distance, even if a message cannot replace a person in the corridor. 🤍

grounding: A quick digital message offers real but thin support in a serious crisis, while a welcomed visit conveys care more fully.

passage:
Subject: Thinking of you, properly this time

Dear Jahnavi,
Last week I sent you a heart emoji and "thinking of you," and afterwards it felt too small for what you are going through with your father. I didn't call because I was afraid of intruding, but I think I hid behind the text as well. So here is a clearer offer. I can bring dinner on Saturday and leave it at the door if you don't want company. Or I can call for a few minutes after your shift. Or you can ignore this email completely and I will understand. Whichever you choose, I'm around, and you don't need to answer quickly.

With care,
Akash

qa.q: What did Akash send Jahnavi last week?
qa.a: A heart emoji and "thinking of you."

qa.q: How did Akash feel about the earlier message, and why?
qa.a: Akash felt the message was too small for what Jahnavi is going through with Jahnavi's father, and had been afraid of intruding, which Akash suspects led to hiding behind the text.

qa.q: What makes Akash's offer easy for Jahnavi to accept or decline?
qa.a: It lists a few choices, including doing nothing, and says there is no need to answer quickly, so Jahnavi keeps control.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi feel reading the email?
qa.a: Jahnavi may feel cared for and relieved to have options, or Jahnavi may still want to be left alone; the email leaves both possible. 🤍

grounding: A heart emoji can seem thin in a serious crisis, so the writer offers a call or a visit that the person is free to welcome or refuse.

passage: I'm Rajni, and I used to carry my friends' problems home like extra luggage. Vishal, a colleague, began staying back after work to talk about his fights with his brother and his exhaustion, and I listened until 10 pm, then lay awake replaying it. One evening I changed how I did it. I said, "It sounds like you feel he never listens to you. Is that right, or is it something else?" Vishal said it was more that he felt ignored than angry. Then I told him, "I can listen for a while tonight, but I can't be the only one you talk to. Have you thought about the counsellor the company offers?" He looked a little hurt, then said he would look at the details. I went home lighter 🙂, and I still text him next morning.

qa.q: What did Vishal say he felt, after Rajni checked a guess?
qa.a: He said it was more that he felt ignored than angry.

qa.q: How was Rajni feeling when asking "Is that right, or is it something else?"
qa.a: Rajni was unsure whether the guess about Vishal's feelings was right, so Rajni checked; his reply that he felt ignored more than angry showed it was only partly right.

qa.q: What did Rajni change that helped Rajni support Vishal?
qa.a: Rajni checked the guess, set a limit on the evening and suggested the company counsellor.

qa.q: How might Vishal have felt when Rajni mentioned the counsellor?
qa.a: He looked a little hurt, perhaps feeling passed along, but he agreed to look at the details, so he may also have found it reasonable.

grounding: A young professional comforts a colleague by checking a guess about his feelings, keeps a limit and refers him to help.

passage: Note from Pranav, team supervisor. On Wednesday I saw Vidya sitting with a colleague who had just received a difficult performance review. She sat at a comfortable distance and let the colleague talk for a while, nodding, before saying, "You sound really discouraged. Am I reading that right?" The colleague said it was more embarrassment than discouragement. Vidya thanked them for correcting her. Later she said, "I'm happy to talk again tomorrow, but I think the company's support service could help with the bigger worry." She gave the colleague the number from the notice board. I noticed Vidya's shoulders were tight afterwards, so I asked how she was. She said she was tired but okay. I have suggested a short break.

qa.q: What did the colleague say the real feeling was?
qa.a: Embarrassment more than discouragement.

qa.q: What might Vidya's tight shoulders suggest about how she felt afterwards?
qa.a: They may suggest she took on some of her colleague's distress and felt tense, though she said she was tired but okay.

qa.q: What could Vidya do to keep supporting others without exhausting herself?
qa.a: She can keep offering to listen while pointing to support services, and take short breaks afterwards, as Pranav suggested. 🙂

qa.q: How might the colleague have felt about Vidya's question "Am I reading that right?"
qa.a: They may have felt understood and free to correct her, since they explained it was embarrassment and not discouragement.

grounding: A young professional listens, checks her reading of a colleague's feelings gently and refers to help, while her own limit shows in her tiredness.

passage: Indu here, Payal's neighbour. Her cousin turned up at the door on Sunday, the one who had borrowed money three times without returning it and once left her stranded at a station. He apologised with his eyes down and asked to start over. Payal listened to all of it. Then she said, "I do forgive you, and I'm not angry any more. But I won't lend money again, and I'd rather we meet at family events than one to one." He nodded, though his jaw tightened. She served him tea at the door, not inside. When he left, she stood there a long time. I couldn't tell whether she felt sad, relieved or both.

qa.q: How many times had the cousin borrowed money without returning it?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: What might Payal have been feeling as she stood at the door after he left?
qa.a: Possibly sadness, relief or both; Indu could not tell, though standing there a long time suggests the conversation cost her something.

qa.q: What could Payal do if he pushes her limits later?
qa.a: She can calmly restate her terms, keep contact to family events, and lean on a trusted person for support if she needs it.

qa.q: How might the cousin have understood Payal's answer?
qa.a: He may have heard both forgiveness and a firm limit, and his tight jaw hints it stung, though he nodded. 🤍

grounding: A young adult forgives while keeping boundaries after repeated broken trust, without being obliged to renew close contact.

passage:
Monday. For the fourth time, Varun had told the group about Pema's job worries after promising not to. He sent a long apology. Pema read it twice and did not reply.
The following Sunday. She wrote, "I accept your apology, and I'm not angry. But this has happened four times, so I'm stepping back from being close. A hello at parties is fine." Varun replied with one line: "I understand."
A month later. At a friend's wedding, Varun nodded from across the room and Pema nodded back. She did not cross over. She felt a small ache and, beneath it, calm.

qa.q: How many times had Varun shared Pema's private worries?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling at the wedding a month later?
qa.a: A small ache with calm beneath it; she nodded back but did not cross the room, so she seemed at peace with her decision though it still hurt a little.

qa.q: What made Pema's message clear and kind?
qa.a: She accepted the apology, said she was not angry, and named what would change, with a hello at parties as the limit.

qa.q: How might Varun have felt on receiving her message?
qa.a: He may have felt regret or hurt, and his short "I understand" could be acceptance or not knowing what else to say.

grounding: A young adult accepts an apology but chooses distance after trust was broken repeatedly, since forgiveness does not oblige renewed closeness.

passage: Jagdish, sitting next to Preeti on Friday. She was about to send the weekly client numbers when she stopped, frowned at her screen and said, "I mixed up two columns in yesterday's file. The totals I sent are wrong for the north region." She went straight to the manager and said, "Yesterday's file had an error, my mistake. I've corrected it and I'm resending it today, and I'll add a second check before I send from now on." The manager said thanks and asked to be copied. Preeti didn't apologise five times or blame the template, though her hands were slightly shaky as she typed. I couldn't tell whether she was scared or just typing fast. By evening the client had the right file.

qa.q: Which region were the wrong totals for?
qa.a: The north region.

qa.q: What might Preeti have been feeling as her hands shook while she typed?
qa.a: She may have been nervous about the mistake, though Jagdish admits it could just be the rush.

qa.q: Why does a short, factual acknowledgement work well here?
qa.a: It states the error, the fix and the new check, so the manager can trust the file without hearing excuses or heavy self-blame. 🙂

qa.q: How might the manager feel about hearing this early?
qa.a: The manager likely felt reassured, having heard it from Preeti before the client noticed, and could plan around the fix.

grounding: A young professional owns an error early, explains the fix and avoids over-apologising or blaming, seen by a colleague.

passage:
Monday. Sunaina realised she had attached last year's price list to a client's quote. She told nobody, hoping the client would not notice.
Wednesday. The client asked why the prices looked old. Vikas, her manager, asked what had happened, and Sunaina said, "The template must have changed." Vikas looked at her for a moment and said nothing more, and the client call was tense.
Next Monday. Sunaina caught another slip, a wrong date on a quote. Within an hour she went to Vikas: "I put the wrong date on the quote. I've fixed it, I've called the client, and I'll resend by noon." Vikas said, "Thanks for telling me right away," and went back to his screen. Her stomach was tight, but it eased.

qa.q: What did Sunaina attach to the client's quote on the first Monday?
qa.a: Last year's price list.

qa.q: What was Sunaina likely feeling when she said "The template must have changed"?
qa.a: She was probably anxious about being blamed and wanted to avoid it, though she may also have been trying to buy time.

qa.q: What did Sunaina change the second time, and why does it help?
qa.a: She reported the slip within an hour with the fix and a time, so Vikas could trust her and plan.

qa.q: How might Vikas have seen her Wednesday answer?
qa.a: Vikas may have doubted it, since he looked at her and said nothing more, though he may simply have been waiting for more.

grounding: A young professional first hides an error and then learns to own one early with a short factual fix, which protects trust.

passage: Reena, you asked why I say "no, no, I'm fine" to the second helping and then look hopeful. Let me tell you about my first visit as a guest. I'm Joseph. I was twenty-four, visiting my friend Suresh's family in Kolkata, and when his mother asked if I wanted more rice I said, "No, thank you," the way we do at home in Kochi, where a guest declines once and the host offers again. Suresh's mother, from a household where a no is a no, nodded and cleared the plate. I went to bed hungry and confused. Now I ask myself what house I'm in, and if I'm unsure, I say, "Maybe a little," the first time.

qa.q: Where was Suresh's family living?
qa.a: In Kolkata.

qa.q: What did Joseph intend by that first "No, thank you"?
qa.a: Joseph meant it politely, expecting the host to offer again as they do at home in Kochi.

qa.q: What can a guest do when unsure about a host's custom?
qa.a: Say "Maybe a little" the first time, so the host has a clear answer without the guest giving up politeness.

qa.q: How did Suresh's mother read the same answer?
qa.a: As a real no, since in her household a no is a no, so she cleared the plate.

grounding: Politeness norms about declining food or help vary, so hosts and guests read a first no cautiously; the guest learns to state a need in a softer, clearer way.

passage: It was past ten and the shops were shut when Hemant reached his colleague Omkar's home for the wedding week. Omkar's mother said, "You must be hungry, sit, sit." Hemant, tired and starving, said, "No, no, please, don't trouble yourself, I ate on the train." He hadn't. She smiled and asked again, "Just a little dal-rice?" He said no again, politely, and looked at the floor. When she asked a third time, he said, "If it's no trouble, a little." A plate arrived at once, holding far more than a little. Omkar, watching, whispered, "She'd have kept asking till midnight." Hemant laughed, relieved, though he wondered if he had seemed greedy.

qa.q: How many times did Hemant say no before he accepted the food?
qa.a: He said no twice, then accepted "a little."

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling when he said "I ate on the train"?
qa.a: He was hungry 😅 but trying to be polite and not trouble the host; looking at the floor could also show shyness.

qa.q: What could Hemant do if he wants to avoid a long wait for food?
qa.a: He can accept on the second offer once he sees the host means it, or say "a little" as he finally did.

qa.q: How might Omkar's mother have read Hemant's first no?
qa.a: Likely as polite hesitation, which is why she asked again, though she could not be sure he did not want food.

grounding: In settings where guests decline food politely before accepting, hosts offer more than once and read context, even under late-night constraints.

passage:
Kavitha: Hi Ayesha, got two minutes? 🙂
Ayesha: Sure, what's up
Kavitha: The client report, is the deadline Thursday or Friday? I'd like to plan my week around it
Ayesha: Thursday end of day
Kavitha: Thanks. Also I'm away Friday to Monday for my cousin's wedding. I'll hand over my open tasks by Wednesday. Would that work?
Ayesha: That works. Send me the list
Kavitha: Will do. One request: after 7 pm, could you message me only for urgent things, and call if it can't wait? I miss chat notifications otherwise 🙏
Ayesha: Fine. Thanks for telling me
Kavitha: 👍

qa.q: When is the client report due?
qa.a: Thursday end of day.

qa.q: How does Kavitha seem to feel about asking for fewer evening messages?
qa.a: Kavitha seems a little hesitant, framing it as "one request" with folded hands, because Kavitha misses chat notifications after 7 pm and wants a call for urgent things.

qa.q: What made Kavitha's requests easy to accept?
qa.a: Kavitha gave a reason and an alternative, such as a Wednesday handover and a call for urgent things.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have felt receiving the requests?
qa.a: Ayesha may have been glad to know the plan early, and Ayesha's short "Fine" could mean agreement or mild reluctance.

grounding: A young professional asks for deadline clarity, leave and a preferred way of being contacted, giving a reason and an alternative.

passage: The cooperative bank's branch in the small town was crowded with farmers on month-end. By afternoon Keerthana's knee ached from standing at the counter. When the noon bus left and the queue thinned, she went to Sahil, the branch manager, who was eating from a steel tiffin. "Sir, I have a request. I need a short sitting break each afternoon because of my knee. I can swap the cash counter with Lakshmi and do the ledger sitting down, so the queue won't suffer." Sahil chewed, then said, "Fine, work it out with Lakshmi." She added, "And if you need me after hours, please call the landline at home, the mobile signal is poor." He nodded, wrote it on the wall calendar, and Keerthana felt her shoulders loosen.

qa.q: What did Keerthana offer to swap with Lakshmi?
qa.a: The cash counter.

qa.q: What might Keerthana have been worried about when she went to Sahil, and what does her reaction suggest?
qa.a: She may have worried he would refuse or fear for the queue; her shoulders loosening afterwards suggests relief.

qa.q: What could Keerthana do next to keep the arrangement working?
qa.a: She can agree the swap times with Lakshmi and tell Sahil if it stops working. 🙂

qa.q: How might Sahil have looked at the request?
qa.a: He may have been weighing the queue and staffing; because Keerthana offered a swap and a reason, the request was easy to grant, and his chewing pause suggests he was considering it.

grounding: A young professional asks for a break accommodation and a preferred way of contact, framing each with a reason and an alternative.

subtype: Indirect disapproval in hierarchical or polite cultures [Mismatch]
passage: So I pitched my inventory dashboard idea to Nitin sir. I'm Varun. He listened, glanced at his phone and said, "We will see." Then he asked about my mother's health. Two days passed and my email got no reply. I spiralled: he hates it, he thinks I'm useless 😔. But a friend told me the same "we will see" from her own boss meant yes-later. So I did something scary. I went over and said, "Sir, I'd like to know whether you want me to keep working on this, or drop it. Either answer is fine." He rubbed his forehead and said, "It's good, but the budget is frozen till next quarter." So the silence was not the no I had imagined.

qa.q: What did Nitin say after Varun's pitch?
qa.a: "We will see."

qa.q: What did Varun fear the silence meant?
qa.a: Varun feared Nitin hated the idea and thought Varun was useless, though the silence turned out to be about the frozen budget, so it could have been hesitation.

qa.q: What made Varun's question to Nitin useful?
qa.a: It asked plainly whether to keep working or drop it, and said either answer was fine, so Nitin could answer honestly.

qa.q: Why might Nitin have said "We will see" and not mentioned the budget?
qa.a: He may have wanted to avoid a plain no out of politeness, or been unsure how to explain the budget.

grounding: Indirect disapproval such as "we will see" and silence is ambiguous and may reflect politeness or hesitation, so the young professional asks gently.

subtype: Indirect disapproval in hierarchical or polite cultures [Mismatch]
passage: Yusuf here, at the next desk. Reena told our department head about her plan to shift her hours earlier. The head listened, smiled and said, "Let me think about it," then asked if she had tried the new canteen. Reena laughed politely, but her fingers kept smoothing her dupatta. I read that as a soft no. A day later the head still hadn't answered her message. Reena said, "Ma'am, would it help if I sent a one-page plan, or would you rather I leave it for now?" The head paused and said, "Send the plan. I'm only waiting on the budget review." Reena thanked her. I had guessed wrong, and I still don't know whether Reena had guessed right from the start.

qa.q: What did the head ask after saying "Let me think about it"?
qa.a: Whether she had tried the new canteen.

qa.q: What might Reena have been feeling as she smoothed her dupatta?
qa.a: Probably uncertain or anxious about whether the reply was a no; Yusuf read a soft no, but it turned out otherwise.

qa.q: What did Reena do that cleared things up?
qa.a: She gently asked whether a one-page plan would help or whether to leave it, giving the head an easy way to answer.

qa.q: How might the head have felt about Reena's question?
qa.a: The head may have felt relieved to explain about the budget review, since the silence was not a no.

grounding: Indirect signals like "let me think about it" and a change of subject are ambiguous, and a gentle question clarified the hierarchy-shaped politeness, seen by a colleague.

subtype: Scolding and reprimanding as a supervisor [Regulating]
passage: I'm Deepak, and I became a shift supervisor at twenty-five. The first time Mahima, one of my juniors, left the packing area unlocked overnight, I nearly said something sharp in front of the team. I felt my voice rising, so I waited until the floor emptied. Then I said, "Last night the packing area was left unlocked from 9 to 6. That put the stock at risk, and I had to explain it to the manager. I'd like you to use the checklist at closing. What would help you remember?" She said the checklist was in the office, not at the door. We moved it. I hadn't used sarcasm or a lecture, and I checked in only once more after that. She hasn't slipped since.

qa.q: Where did Mahima say the checklist was kept?
qa.a: In the office, not at the door.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling before he spoke to Mahima, and how did Deepak handle it?
qa.a: Deepak felt irritated and noticed the rising voice, so Deepak waited until the floor emptied and spoke calmly.

qa.q: What made Deepak's reprimand more effective than a sharp remark in front of the team?
qa.a: Deepak described the behaviour and its impact, stayed calm and asked what would help, so Mahima could fix the problem without humiliation.

qa.q: How might Mahima have felt if Deepak had scolded her in front of the team?
qa.a: She might have felt humiliated and defensive, and been less willing to say the checklist was in the wrong place.

grounding: A young supervisor reprimands by describing the behaviour and its impact, keeping calm and giving a path to improve.

subtype: Scolding and reprimanding as a supervisor [Regulating]
passage: Note from Uma, operations head. I observed Jaya, a new supervisor, speak to a trainee about repeated late arrivals. Jaya took the trainee aside, away from the others, and said in an even voice, "For three mornings you've come after the briefing started. The team has had to repeat the instructions for you, and it slows the start. I want you here by the briefing. Is something making it hard?" The trainee explained about the bus timetable. Jaya offered to move the trainee to the later group for two weeks and to review then. There was no sarcasm and no raised voice. Afterwards Jaya asked me if she had been too soft. I told her that clear and calm is not soft, and suggested she write the review date down.

qa.q: How many mornings had the trainee arrived after the briefing began?
qa.a: Three mornings.

qa.q: What was Jaya worried about when she asked Uma if she had been too soft?
qa.a: She worried that being calm and kind might not be firm enough; Uma's answer suggests her approach was fine.

qa.q: What could Jaya do to make sure the plan works?
qa.a: She can write down the review date and check in then, as Uma suggested.

qa.q: How might the trainee have felt being spoken to away from the others?
qa.a: They probably felt less embarrassed and more able to explain about the bus timetable.

grounding: A young supervisor reprimands calmly, describing the behaviour and its impact, listening to the cause and offering a path to improve, seen by a senior.
